args.query: What operation combines the identity shortcut with the residual branch in an original ResNet identity block?
Which layer outputs does a DenseNet layer receive inside a dense block?
What direct architectural implication follows from ResNet using addition versus DenseNet using concatenation for feature combination?

args.instructions: Answer the question directly in the first sentence. Then compare what each paper says, naming the paper for every point, and state where the papers agree, disagree or report numbers that are not comparable. If one hop of the question is not answered by the evidence, say which.

result.answer:
Answer: In the original ResNet (1512.03385v1), an identity block combines the shortcut with the residual branch by element-wise addition [S:43eecbafc161#21][S:43eecbafc161#22]; in DenseNet (1608.06993v5), each layer inside a dense block receives all preceding feature-maps as input [S:20e50960076d#8], and input concatenation directly lets earlier feature-maps be accessed by all subsequent layers, encouraging feature reuse and more compact models [S:20e50960076d#69].

Explanation: ResNet (1512.03385v1, p. 3) defines the block as “y = F(x, {Wi}) + x” [S:43eecbafc161#21] and says “The operation F + x is performed by a shortcut connection and element-wise addition” [S:43eecbafc161#22]; its element-wise addition is performed on two feature maps channel by channel [S:43eecbafc161#23], and its shortcut introduces neither extra parameter nor computation complexity [S:43eecbafc161#22]. DenseNet (1608.06993v5, p. 1) says “Each layer takes all preceding feature-maps as input” [S:20e50960076d#8], and on p. 4 it describes each layer as having access to all preceding feature-maps in its block, adding k feature-maps to the network’s global state [S:20e50960076d#35]. One direct architectural implication is stated on p. 7: “As a direct consequence of the input concatenation, the feature-maps learned by any of the DenseNet layers can be accessed by all subsequent layers,” which encourages feature reuse and more compact models [S:20e50960076d#69]. A further concatenation-specific consequence is that the operation is “not viable when the size of feature-maps changes,” so DenseNet uses transition layers between dense blocks [S:20e50960076d#28]. The papers are consistent in treating connectivity as beneficial—ResNet’s identity shortcuts are parameter-free [S:43eecbafc161#15], while DenseNet emphasizes improved information and gradient flow [S:20e50960076d#14]—but they differ operationally: addition in ResNet [S:43eecbafc161#22] versus concatenation in DenseNet [S:20e50960076d#28]. For numbers, the DenseNet paper reports “DenseNets achieve lower error rates while using fewer parameters than ResNet” [S:20e50960076d#43], a model-level performance comparison; the operation-level descriptions remain addition [S:43eecbafc161#22] and concatenation [S:20e50960076d#28].

3.2. Identity Mapping by Shortcuts
We adopt residual learning to every few stacked layers.
A building block is shown in Fig. 2. Formally, in this paper
we consider a building block deﬁned as:
y = F(x, {Wi}) + x.
(1)
Here x and y are the input and output vectors of the lay-
ers considered.
The function F(x, {Wi}) represents the
residual mapping to be learned. For the example in Fig. 2
that has two layers, F = W2σ(W1x) in which σ denotes
2This hypothesis, however, is still an open question. See [28].

citations.text:
ReLU [29] and the biases are omitted for simplifying no-
tations. The operation F + x is performed by a shortcut
connection and element-wise addition. We adopt the sec-
ond nonlinearity after the addition (i.e., σ(y), see Fig. 2).
The shortcut connections in Eqn.(1) introduce neither ex-
tra parameter nor computation complexity. This is not only
attractive in practice but also important in our comparisons
between plain and residual networks. We can fairly com-
pare plain/residual networks that simultaneously have the
same number of parameters, depth, width, and computa-
tional cost (except for the negligible element-wise addition).
The dimensions of x and F must be equal in Eqn.(1).
If this is not the case (e.g., when changing the input/output
channels), we can perform a linear projection Ws by the
shortcut connections to match the dimensions:
y = F(x, {Wi}) + Wsx.
(2)

citations.text:
We can also use a square matrix Ws in Eqn.(1). But we will
show by experiments that the identity mapping is sufﬁcient
for addressing the degradation problem and is economical,
and thus Ws is only used when matching dimensions.
The form of the residual function F is ﬂexible. Exper-
iments in this paper involve a function F that has two or
three layers (Fig. 5), while more layers are possible. But if
F has only a single layer, Eqn.(1) is similar to a linear layer:
y = W1x + x, for which we have not observed advantages.
We also note that although the above notations are about
fully-connected layers for simplicity, they are applicable to
convolutional layers. The function F(x, {Wi}) can repre-
sent multiple convolutional layers. The element-wise addi-
tion is performed on two feature maps, channel by channel.

Pooling layers.
The concatenation operation used in
Eq. (2) is not viable when the size of feature-maps changes.
However, an essential part of convolutional networks is
down-sampling layers that change the size of feature-maps.
To facilitate down-sampling in our architecture we divide
the network into multiple densely connected dense blocks;
see Figure 2. We refer to layers between blocks as transition
layers, which do convolution and pooling. The transition
layers used in our experiments consist of a batch normal-
ization layer and an 1×1 convolutional layer followed by a
2×2 average pooling layer.

Shortcut Connections. Practices and theories that lead to
shortcut connections [2, 34, 49] have been studied for a long
time. An early practice of training multi-layer perceptrons
(MLPs) is to add a linear layer connected from the network
input to the output [34, 49]. In [44, 24], a few interme-
diate layers are directly connected to auxiliary classiﬁers
for addressing vanishing/exploding gradients. The papers
of [39, 38, 31, 47] propose methods for centering layer re-
sponses, gradients, and propagated errors, implemented by
shortcut connections. In [44], an “inception” layer is com-
posed of a shortcut branch and a few deeper branches.
Concurrent with our work, “highway networks” [42, 43]
present shortcut connections with gating functions [15].
These gates are data-dependent and have parameters, in
contrast to our identity shortcuts that are parameter-free.
